title: Effective agent design patterns in production — Laurie Voss, LlamaIndex
talk_summary: The practical core is composing simple LLM/tool steps, using parallel checks or votes to reduce hallucination, and looping evaluator feedback to improve outputs.

takeaways.what_they_do: Run the same review prompt through multiple independent model tracks and aggregate by majority or unanimous vote to suppress model-specific hallucinations.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you know three different LLMs come to the same conclusion, then it's probably not the LLM just making stuff up

takeaways.what_they_do: A separate LLM judge compares output to the original goal, returns feedback, and loops back to the producing step.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can get the LLM to generate feedback and send it back

takeaways.what_they_do: An orchestrator LLM splits a complex task into simpler independent questions, runs them in parallel, then aggregates answers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: split it into several simpler questions and ask each of those questions in parallel

takeaways.what_they_do: Use retrieval to send only relevant context instead of stuffing the whole corpus, because less context is cheaper/faster and more specific.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's always going to be cheaper and faster to send less data that the LLM has to think about less

takeaways.what_they_do: Give an LLM/router decision power over which tool or path to use for different problem types.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you give the LLM decision-making power to say which of these tools should I call

takeaways.what_they_do: Run a second parallel LLM track that checks whether the request or action violates rules while the main track processes it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you use the second one of your tracks to query is this an illegal request?
